records.issue_text: [BUG] OrderedQueueWorker.run() marks an offset complete in the finally block even when result_processor raised, so the commit loop advances the Kafka offset past messages whose processing failed. The class docstring and strategy guarantee "Only commits offsets after successful processing" is violated: any transient failure (DB error, timeout) in result_processor permanently drops that uptime result with no retry and no dead-letter, because the failed offset is immediately committable; the test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling test even encodes this silent data loss without asserting it. A crash-retry loop that the serial mode provides is silently removed in this mode.

Every existing test uses sequential or low-contention access, so this race is unverified.

An Arroyo caller invoking join(timeout=1) during a stall (e.g., a stuck result_processor) blocks for up to 5 + 5*num_queues seconds instead of honoring the deadline, converting a graceful rebalance into a consumer-group timeout; the parameter is a silent no-op that misleads the next maintainer.
records.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(self, timeout: float | None = None)`, the `timeout` parameter is ignored and it unconditionally calls `self.close()` (see `def join(...): self.close()`). `close()` then joins `self.commit_thread` with a hardcoded `timeout=5.0`, and `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` joins each worker with `timeout=5.0` serially. This makes `join(timeout=...)` a silent no-op and can block far longer than the caller-supplied timeout, matching the finding’s mechanism.

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool uses unbounded queue.Queue instances, so the docstring claim of "Natural backpressure when queues fill up" is not enforced anywhere. If result processing falls behind consumption (Kafka lag spike, slow handle_result), submit() keeps enqueueing without bound and the process grows memory until OOM; operators of uptime consumers running thread-queue-parallel get killed workers instead of the backpressure the design promises.
records.rationale: The new `FixedQueuePool` constructs each work queue as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (unbounded) (`work_queue: queue.Queue[...] = queue.Queue()`), and `submit()` always does `work_queue.put(work_item)` with no capacity checks/blocking. However, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`’s docstring explicitly claims “Natural backpressure when queues fill up”. With unbounded queues, they never “fill up”, so consumption can enqueue indefinitely if workers fall behind, leading to unbounded memory growth/OOM. This is a verifiable behavior mismatch introduced by this diff.

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join() is implemented as close(), collapsing arroyo's distinct join/wait-for-drain phase into a shutdown that stops the commit thread and shuts down the queue pool. During a rebalance or processor stop, arroyo calls join() to wait for in-flight messages to finish; here join immediately terminates the commit loop before queued items drain, so in-flight work items are discarded without a final offset commit, causing reprocessing at startup — inconsistent with the other strategies' drain semantics and a behavior change nobody explicitly accepted.
records.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(self, timeout: float | None = None)`, the `timeout` parameter is ignored and it unconditionally calls `self.close()` (see `def join(...): self.close()`). `close()` then joins `self.commit_thread` with a hardcoded `timeout=5.0`, and `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` joins each worker with `timeout=5.0` serially. This makes `join(timeout=...)` a silent no-op and can block far longer than the caller-supplied timeout, matching the finding’s mechanism.

records.issue_text: [BUG] OrderedQueueWorker.run marks an offset complete in the finally block even when result_processor raised, so failed messages have their offsets committed and are permanently dropped. A transient DB/network error (or a poison payload) during uptime result processing causes the message to be logged and its offset committed; on restart the consumer resumes past it, so the check result is silently lost with no retry and no dead-letter path — the 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' guarantee stated in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's docstring is false.
records.rationale: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, the `finally` block always calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` even if `result_processor(...)` raised an exception (it is caught/logged in the `except Exception:` block). Since `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets()` treats any offset that is no longer “outstanding” as processed, the commit loop in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop` can advance commits past failed messages with no retry/DLQ, contradicting the strategy docstring guarantee “Only commits offsets after successful processing.”

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] OffsetTracker._get_partition_lock has a check-then-set race: two threads calling it concurrently for a new partition can each construct a different Lock, with partition_locks.setdefault keeping only one, so one thread proceeds with an unlocked guard. During consumer startup or rebalance, concurrent add_offset/complete_offset calls for a newly-seen partition can mutate the offset sets without mutual exclusion, producing a corrupted outstanding set and an incorrectly computed committable offset (over-commit → message loss). Rebuttal: callers mostly hit the same partition repeatedly after the first insert, so the window is narrow — but the first two messages on a partition arrive via separate worker threads and strategy submit simultaneously, so the trigger exists in this diff's own call pattern.

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] OrderedQueueWorker.run executes result_processor with sentry_sdk.start_transaction but no isolation/scope handling, and worker exceptions are swallowed with only a log, so a worker thread that dies is never replaced. The thread is a daemon with no supervisor; if run() exits other than via the shutdown flag (e.g., an unexpected BaseException or future edit), all messages for the groups hashed to that queue block forever while the offset tracker never completes them, stalling all offset commits for those partitions with only an exception log as forensics — operators see the consumer as healthy-but-stuck.

records.issue_text: [BUG] test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts that no offsets are committed after a processing failure, but the implementation commits them anyway, so the test can only pass by winning a race against the 1-second commit loop. OrderedQueueWorker.run completes the offset in a finally block even when result_processor raises, so the errored message's offset becomes committable and _commit_loop (waking every 1.0s) will commit past it. The test's final assertion `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` is checked only ~0.2s after processing finishes — it passes only when the commit loop hasn't fired yet, so the suite gives false confidence that errors block commits while the code actually commits past failures (which for uptime results means silently losing the failed message). On a slow CI box the commit thread fires first and the test flakes; on the code's real semantics the assertion is simply wrong.

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] test_different_groups_distributed asserts `len(queue_indices) == 3` based on Python's per-process randomized str hash, making the test flaky across PYTHONHASHSEED values. get_queue_for_group uses built-in hash() on strings, which is salted per process; the 20 group keys could all collide into 2 (or 1) of the 3 queues for some seeds (probability ≈ 2·(2/3)^20 ≈ 0.5% per run), producing an intermittent CI failure that no code change explains. More importantly, the assertion verifies an accidental hash-distribution property rather than the ordering guarantee, so it tests the mock-machinery of hashing rather than the spec.

The diff's own error-handling test only passes because it checks committed_offsets before the 1s commit tick fires.

records.issue_text: [BUG] The docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up" but every queue is constructed with `queue.Queue()` (no maxsize), so there is no backpressure and memory grows without bound. If result processing is slower than Kafka consumption (slow DB, incident on one hot subscription serializing behind one worker), submit() never blocks, arroyo keeps polling, and WorkItems (including full decoded payloads) accumulate in unbounded in-process queues until the consumer OOMs — with offsets uncommitted, so restart replays the whole backlog.
records.rationale: The new `FixedQueuePool` constructs each work queue as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (unbounded) (`work_queue: queue.Queue[...] = queue.Queue()`), and `submit()` always does `work_queue.put(work_item)` with no capacity checks/blocking. However, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`’s docstring explicitly claims “Natural backpressure when queues fill up”. With unbounded queues, they never “fill up”, so consumption can enqueue indefinitely if workers fall behind, leading to unbounded memory growth/OOM. This is a verifiable behavior mismatch introduced by this diff.

Each of the 20 worker threads holds its own persistent Django DB connection that is never closed or refreshed; after a database restart/failover the connections go stale and every subsequent result on those workers raises, which combined with the finally-completes-offset behavior converts a transient DB blip into permanent message loss. Also multiplied DB connection counts per consumer process.
